claims.claim: It can be right to lie in order to protect someone.

stances.summary: Deceit is not evil in itself; it is judged by the intention behind it. Deceiving someone to save or help them is good, and Michal saved David from Saul only by deceiving her father.
stances.quote: For the daughter of Saul would not have been able to rescue her husband out of Saul's hands except by deceiving her father. And her brother, wishing to save him whom she had rescued when he was again in danger, made use of the same weapon as the wife.
stances.translation: W. R. W. Stephens, NPNF series 1 vol. 9, 1889 (as revised for New Advent)
stances.original: Καὶ γὰρ τῶν τοῦ Σαοὺλ χειρῶν ἡ τοῦ Σαοὺλ θυγάτηρ οὐκ ἴσχυσεν ἂν ἑτέρως ἐξελέσθαι τὸν ἄνδρα τὸν αὑτῆς, ἀλλ' ἢ μετὰ τοῦ παραλογίσασθαι τὸν πατέρα· ὁ ταύτης δὲ ἀδελφὸς τὸν ὑπ' ἐκείνης διασωθέντα σῶσαι βουλόμενος κινδυνεύοντα πάλιν τοῖς αὐτοῖς ὅπλοις ἐχρῆτο οἷσπερ καὶ ἡ γυνή.
stances.location: Book 1, section 8 in the NPNF numbering (often cited as 1.8-9)
stances.context: Written c. 386-390 as a dialogue with his friend Basil (not Basil the Great). Chrysostom had let Basil believe they would both accept ordination, then hid, so Basil alone was ordained. Chrysostom defends this: 'if the evil of deception is absolute, and it is never right to make use of it, I am prepared to pay any penalty', but deceit 'becomes good or bad according to the intention of those who practise it'. He cites generals, physicians who trick feverish patients, Michal and Jonathan saving David, and Paul circumcising Timothy, and concludes: 'For great is the value of deceit, provided it be not introduced with a mischievous intention.' Also: 'often it is necessary to deceive', and whoever refuses may do 'great mischief to the person whom he has not deceived'. His Greek word throughout is apate (deceit), never pseudos (lie), and he says such deceit should rather be called 'economy' (oikonomia). His own deceit included a misleading promise, so it was a spoken untruth. The case he chose (Michal lying to Saul to save David) is exactly lying to protect a life. No later retraction is known. Greek from melodos.com (PG text), chapters headed 'That it is right to use deceit for a good end' and 'That such a thing should not even be called deceit, but economy'.

stances.summary: A lie is like hellebore: deadly as daily food, life-saving as a last resort. If murderers ask where people are hiding, love of neighbour obliges us to lie rather than hand them over, though we should feel humbled for it.
stances.quote: For if we seek our own, and want obstinately to keep what is good for ourselves, we must even in urgent cases of this sort speak the truth, and so become guilty of the death of another: but if we prefer what is for another's advantage to our own good, and satisfy the demands of the Apostle, we shall certainly have to put up with the necessity of lying.
stances.translation: Edgar C. S. Gibson, NPNF series 2 vol. 11, 1894 (as revised for New Advent)
stances.original: si uero ea quae aliis salutaria sunt nostris utilitatibus praeponentes apostolico satisfecerimus imperio, sine dubio subeunda est nobis necessitas mentiendi. (Latin of the second half only, reconstructed from a poor OCR of Petschenig's CSEL 13, 1886, p. 481; check against a clean edition before printing)
stances.work: Conferences (Conference 17, the second conference of Abbot Joseph, 'On making promises')
stances.context: Written c. 426-429. The words are put in the mouth of Abba Joseph of Panephysis in Egypt; Cassian presents them approvingly as the teaching of the desert elders. The chapter asks the reader directly what he would do if, like the woman who hid David's messengers in a well (2 Samuel 17), he could save hunted men only by a lie: 'would you prefer to hide them with a similar falsehood ... or by speaking the truth, would you have given up those in hiding to the men who would kill them?' Chapter 17: 'we ought to regard a lie and to employ it as if its nature were that of hellebore', and 'When then any grave danger hangs on confession of the truth, then we must take to lying as a refuge, yet in such a way as to be for our salvation troubled by the guilt of a humbled conscience.' Cassian praises Rahab's lie and condemns Delilah's truth-telling. Chapters 21-24 go further and allow small lies to hide one's own fasting from others. Strong qualification: only in 'the utmost necessity', otherwise 'most carefully avoided as if it were something deadly'. Cassian is orthodox and honoured East and West, though his Conference 13 was attacked in the West on grace.

stances.summary: In this wicked world a lie is often necessary, as when we lie to a killer about someone in hiding. Scripture forbids the lie that harms a neighbour, not the one that saves him.
stances.quote: But this is a narrow way, and hard amid the wickedness and vices of the world. For a lie is often necessary, and falsehood is sometimes useful: when we lie to a killer about someone in hiding, or frustrate testimony for someone in danger, or deceive a sick man about how hard his cure will be.
stances.translation: own rendering from the Latin of CSEL 22 (A. Zingerle, 1891), p. 91
stances.original: Sed artum hoc et per saeculi nequitias ac uitia difficile est. est enim necessarium plerumque mendacium, et nonnumquam falsitas utilis est, cum aut percussori de latente mentimur, aut testimonium pro periclitante frustramur, aut fallimus de difficultate curationis aegrotum; et oportet secundum apostoli doctrinam sermonem nostrum sale esse conditum, idcirco nunc spiritus sanctus falsitatis adfectum mendacii condicionibus temperauit dicens: qui non egit dolum in lingua sua nec fecit proximo suo malum, ut crimen mendacii in incommodo haberetur alieno.
stances.work: Tractates on the Psalms (Tractatus super Psalmos), on Psalm 14 (15 in Hebrew numbering)
stances.context: Written c. 364-367, by an orthodox bishop, the leading Latin opponent of Arianism. Commenting on Psalm 15:3 ('who has not done deceit with his tongue, nor done evil to his neighbour'), he says the Holy Spirit 'tempered' the ban on falsehood with conditions, 'so that the crime of lying would be reckoned by the harm done to another'. So in his reading only the harmful lie is condemned. The first example he gives is exactly the protective lie: lying to a killer (percussor) about someone hidden. There is no pre-1929 English of this tractate (NPNF vol. 9 translates only Psalms 1, 53 and 130), hence the own rendering. The url is archive.org's OCR of the 1891 edition: the Latin there is broken across lines with line numbers and hyphens ('nonnum- quam', 'men- 5 timur'), so match the 'original' field after removing them. 'frustramur' is rendered literally ('frustrate'); it means making testimony fail or mislead to help someone in peril.

stances.summary: God never lies, but for human beings a lie can sometimes be needed, like a medicine. Whoever is forced to lie must do it with great care, only for some great good, as Judith, Esther and Jacob did.
stances.quote: But a man on whom necessity imposes the responsibility of lying is bound to use very great care, and to use falsehood as he would a stimulant or a medicine, and strictly to preserve its measure, and not go beyond the bounds observed by Judith in her dealings with Holofernes
stances.translation: W. H. Fremantle, NPNF series 2 vol. 3, 1892 (English of Jerome's Latin quotation of Origen)
stances.work: Stromateis (Miscellanies), book 6 (lost in Greek), quoted by Jerome in Apology against Rufinus
stances.location: Jerome, Apology against Rufinus, book 1, section 18
stances.context: Origen's Stromateis are lost; this fragment survives only because Jerome quoted it in 401 to discredit Origen and his followers, so the source is hostile, but the words are given as Origen's own. Origen is adapting Plato's Republic, book 3, where lies are useful to men 'as a medicine'. He adds: 'From all this it is evident that if we speak falsely with any other object than that of obtaining by it some great good, we shall be judged as the enemies of him who said, I am the truth.' Examples: Judith with Holofernes, Esther hiding her race, Jacob winning the blessing. Not framed specifically as protecting another person, but 'some great good' and 'necessity' plainly include it. In Against Celsus 4.19 he also allows that deceit may work 'by way, as it were, of medicine', but there he is conceding Celsus's own premise, so that passage is weaker evidence. Origen's teachings were condemned after his death (6th century); mark him as heterodox. Jerome's closing gloss ('the master may lie, but the disciple must not') is Jerome's sarcasm, not Origen.

stances.person: Alonius (Abba Alonis, desert father of Scetis)
stances.summary: If you refuse ever to lie, you will commit many sins. If a man flees to you and the judge asks whether you saw him, telling the truth hands him over to death; better to let him go and leave him to God's judgement.
stances.quote: If thou dost not lie, thou art about to commit many sins.
stances.translation: E. A. Wallis Budge, The Paradise or Garden of the Holy Fathers, vol. 2, 1907 (from the Syriac of Anan-Isho)
stances.work: Sayings of the Desert Fathers (Apophthegmata; Greek alphabetical collection, Alonius 4)
stances.location: Budge, Paradise vol. 2, Book 1, chapter 8 ('Of Scrupulous Watchfulness'), saying 391
stances.context: Abba Agathon asked how to keep his tongue from falsehood. Alonius gives the case: two brethren commit a murder, one flees to you, the judge asks 'Did this murder take place in thy presence?' and 'if thou dost not wish to tell a lie thou wilt deliver up to death the other man, whom it would be right for thee to let go free, so that he might be reserved for the judgement hall of God, Who knoweth all things.' Note: the person protected is guilty, not innocent; the point is mercy and leaving judgement to God. The sayings were collected in the 5th century from the oral tradition of the elders (Alonius flourished late 4th/early 5th c.). Wikisource's transcription has a typo, 'tell a I lie', in the longer sentence; the quote chosen avoids it.

stances.person: Ammonas (Abba Ammon, disciple of Antony, later bishop)
stances.summary: To shield a sinning brother from a crowd come to expose him, the elder hid the evidence and let the crowd believe it was not there, then warned the brother privately.
stances.quote: Abbâ Ammon, understanding what that brother had done, for the sake of God hid the matter. And he went in and sat upon the earthenware vessel, and commanded that the cell of the brother should be searched, but although they examined the place they found no one there.
stances.translation: E. A. Wallis Budge, The Paradise or Garden of the Holy Fathers, vol. 2, 1907 (from the Syriac of Anan-Isho)
stances.work: Sayings of the Desert Fathers (Greek alphabetical collection, Ammonas 10)
stances.location: Budge, Paradise vol. 2, Book 1, chapter 9 ('Of Love, and Charity'), saying 400
stances.context: A brother had a woman in his cell; the villagers gathered to expel him and asked Ammon to come. The brother hid her under a jar; Ammon sat on the jar, had the cell searched, then said to the crowd 'What is this that ye have done? May God forgive you', and afterwards told the brother privately 'Take heed to thy soul'. This is deception by action and by a misleading rebuke, not an explicit false statement, and it protects a guilty brother from shame rather than a life from death. Hence strength 1. Told as praise of his mercy. 5th-century collection of 4th-century sayings.

stances.summary: The true Christian speaks the truth and will not lie even for a neighbour he loves. Yet like a doctor he may, for the safety of those in his care, deceive or say something untrue.
stances.quote: For he both thinks and speaks the truth; unless at any time, medicinally, as a physician for the safety of the sick, he may deceive or tell an untruth, according to the Sophists.
stances.translation: William Wilson, ANF vol. 2, 1885 (as revised for New Advent)
stances.context: Written c. 200. Two sides in two adjacent chapters. Chapter 8 says the perfect Christian will not lie 'for the sake of the neighbour whom he has learned to love', nor deny the truth 'though he should die by tortures'. Chapter 9 then allows the teacher to 'deceive or tell an untruth' medicinally, 'as a physician for the safety of the sick', citing Paul circumcising Timothy, and ends that he is 'never willing to lie by uttered word'. Scholars read him as allowing therapeutic deception (the Platonic 'medicinal lie') while forbidding ordinary lying. He does not discuss hiding someone from a killer. Hence 'mixed'.

stances.summary: Liars excuse themselves as imitators of Rahab, saving others at their own ruin; that is self-deception. Only when we are wholly cleansed of lying may we resort to it, with fear, when the moment truly calls.
stances.quote: When we have been wholly cleansed of lying, then let us have recourse to it, with fear, and when the occasion calls for it.
stances.translation: own rendering from the Greek text published by St Catherine's Monastery, Sinai
stances.original: Ὁπόταν ψεύδους εἰς ἅπαν καθαρεύσωμεν, τότε αὐτὸ μετὰ φόβου καὶ καιροῦ καλοῦντος ὑπέλθωμεν.
stances.location: Step 12 ('On lying'), sections 7-8 in the Sinai Greek numbering
stances.context: Written c. 600 at Sinai. Section 7 (own rendering): 'The one who puts forward lies pleads economy, and often counts the ruin of the soul as righteousness. The fabricator of lies makes himself out to be an imitator of Rahab, and says he is working another's salvation through his own ruin.' Greek: 'προφασίζεται οἰκονομίας ὁ ψεύδους προβολεύς ... Τῆς Ῥαὰβ μιμητὴν ἑαυτὸν τεκμαίρεσθαι ψευδοπλάστης ἀνήρ, καὶ δι' ἀπωλείας οἰκείας τὴν ἑτέραν σωτηρίαν λέγει πραγματεύεσθαι.' So he distrusts the protective-lie excuse, yet in section 8 leaves a door open for the purified. Section 2: 'Let no one of sound mind think the sin of lying is a small one.' The only English translations are post-1929 (Moore 1959, Luibheid 1982), hence the own rendering. Modern translations number these lines differently.

stances.summary: Every lie is a sin, even one told to save a life. If someone is hiding with you and the pursuer asks, say 'I know where he is, but I will never show you', and bear the consequences.
stances.quote: How much braver then, how much more excellent, to say, I will neither betray nor lie?
stances.translation: H. Browne, NPNF series 1 vol. 3, 1887 (as revised for New Advent)
stances.original: Quanto ergo fortius, quanto excellentius dices: Nec prodam, nec mentiar?
stances.context: The strongest and most sustained voice on this side: two whole treatises, On Lying (c. 395) and Against Lying (c. 420), plus Enchiridion 18-22 (c. 421). He works through the exact case of a man hiding in your house from those who would kill him. His answer: neither lie nor betray; say 'I know where he is, but I will never show' (section 24) and suffer whatever follows, which he calls 'not only not culpable, but even laudable'. He praises Bishop Firmus of Thagaste, who was tortured rather than lie or hand over a fugitive (section 23). He admits the question is very hard and that those who 'never lie except to save a man from injury' have 'attained a very high standard of goodness', but 'it is not the deceit, but their good intention, that is justly praised' and the deception is only to be 'pardoned' (Enchiridion 22). On the Hebrew midwives and Rahab: 'That therefore which was rewarded in them was, not their deceit, but their benevolence' (Against Lying 32). No change of mind; the later works are firmer. Latin from augustinus.it.

stances.summary: A lie told to save a life is the lightest kind of lie and easily forgiven, but it is still a sin, and the perfect will not lie even to save someone's life.
stances.quote: This kind of lying also those that are perfect eschew with the greatest care, so that not even the life of any man should by deceit of theirs be defended, lest they hurt their own souls, whilst they busy themselves to give life to another’s flesh
stances.translation: Library of the Fathers, Morals on the Book of Job, vol. 2 (Oxford: John Henry Parker, 1844-50); translator not named on the page
stances.original: hoc quoque mendacii genus perfecti viri summopere fugiunt, ut nec vita cujuslibet per eorum fallaciam defendatur, ne suae animae noceant, dum praestare vitam carni nituntur alienae
stances.work: Morals on the Book of Job (Moralia in Iob)
stances.context: Written c. 578-595. He grants that 'there is a certain sort of lying which is of lighter complexion, if a man lie in rendering good', and that it is 'very easily remitted', but the perfect avoid it. On the Hebrew midwives (section 6): God 'made them houses', yet 'the profits of their kindness which might have been repaid them in everlasting life, on account of the sin of lying mixing in are diverted into an earthly recompense'. He adds that Old Testament lies belonged to a time of shadows, and the New Testament asks more. Follows Augustine closely; this became the standard Western medieval position. The page is encoded windows-1252 and its apostrophe in 'another’s' is a curly one (byte 0x92); decode it as windows-1252 when checking. Latin from la.wikisource (Moralia part IV).

stances.summary: No lie is allowed, even for some good end. The Lord said once for all that lying is of the devil and made no exceptions.
stances.quote: It is forbidden by the decision of the Lord Who said once for all that lying is of the devil, and allowed no difference in lying.
stances.translation: W. K. Lowther Clarke, The Ascetic Works of Saint Basil (London: SPCK), 1925
stances.location: Question 76: 'Is it lawful to lie in order to achieve some supposed good?'
stances.context: Written for Basil's monastic communities in the 360s-370s, in question-and-answer form. The question covers any 'supposed good', which includes protecting someone, though Basil does not discuss the killer-at-the-door case. The answer continues by citing 2 Timothy 2:5 (no crown unless one contends lawfully). His Morals, rule 24, likewise: 'That one must not lie but must speak the truth in everything.' The url is archive.org's OCR of Clarke's 1925 book, which misreads two characters in this sentence ('It 1s', and a footnote mark read as '®' after 'devil'); the quote gives the printed text. Clarke's 1925 English is public domain in the US (published before 1929) but Clarke died in 1968, so it is still in copyright in the UK until 2038. Basil is the notable Greek absolutist against the Eastern trend.

stances.summary: The just man never lies, not even to an enemy or a stranger. In the way of justice there is no room for falsehood.
stances.quote: For it is unlawful for him who cultivates truth to be deceitful in anything, and to depart from the truth itself which he follows. In this path of justice and all the virtues there is no place for falsehood.
stances.translation: William Fletcher, ANF vol. 7, 1886 (as revised for New Advent)
stances.original: Est enim nefas, eum, qui veritati studeat, in aliqua re esse fallacem; atque ab ipsa, quam sequitur, veritate discedere. In hâc justitiae virtutumque omnium via, nullus mendacio locus est.
stances.context: Written c. 303-311. The sentence before says no one should 'ever speak falsely for the sake of deceiving or injuring' (Latin 'decipiendi aut nocendi causa'), which some could read as a loophole, but the lines that follow close it: 'he will think that it is not his part to speak falsely even to an enemy and a stranger; nor will he at any time so act, that his tongue, which is the interpreter of his mind, should be at variance with his feeling and thought.' A general rule, not a ruling on the hiding case, hence strength 1. Latin from remacle.org.

stances.person: John of Lycopolis (desert hermit of the Thebaid)
stances.summary: A lie is a lie whether it is about something small or great, or simply convenient, and it is never to be praised.
stances.quote: for falsehood, whether it be uttered concerning a small matter or a great one, or something which is convenient, is still falsehood, and is not to be praised.
stances.translation: E. A. Wallis Budge, The Paradise or Garden of the Holy Fathers, vol. 1, 1907 (from the Syriac version of the History of the Monks)
stances.work: History of the Monks in Egypt (Historia monachorum in Aegypto), the chapter on John of Lycopolis
stances.location: Budge, Paradise vol. 1, History of the Monks, chapter 2 (chapter 1 in the Greek)
stances.context: Recorded by the group of pilgrims who visited John c. 394-395, shortly before his death: an eyewitness record. The lie in question was a deacon's humble denial of his own rank, not a lie to protect someone else, so this shows the Egyptian absolutist line, not a ruling on the hiding case; hence strength 1. It contrasts directly with Cassian, Conference 17.21-24, who allows exactly this kind of humble lie.

stances.summary: Asked under torture to give up a man hiding with him, the bishop answered that he could neither lie nor betray a man.
stances.quote: he made answer to their questions, that he could neither tell a lie, nor betray a man; and when he had suffered so many torments of body, (for as yet emperors were not Christian,) he stood firm in his purpose.
stances.translation: H. Browne, NPNF series 1 vol. 3, 1887 (as revised for New Advent)
stances.original: respondit quaerentibus nec mentiri se posse, nec hominem prodere, passusque tam multa tormenta corporis (nondum enim erant Imperatores christiani), permansit in sententia.
stances.context: CAUTION: these are Augustine's words reporting Firmus, written c. 395, generations after the event (before the Christian emperors, so before c. 312). Nothing of Firmus survives in his own hand, and this is not a near-contemporary record. Augustine adds that the emperor, admiring him, pardoned the man he was protecting. Useful as an illustration of the absolutist ideal, not as a quiz result.

splits_fathers: Real voices on both sides, and roughly even among those who addressed it. For a protective or 'necessary' lie: Hilary (bluntly, with the killer-at-the-door example), Chrysostom (Michal saving David), Cassian and his Abba Joseph (the hellebore image, and the explicit hiding case), Origen (heterodox; lies as medicine), the desert elders Alonius and Ammonas. In the middle: Clement (no lie for a neighbour, but a physician's untruth allowed) and Climacus (mocks the Rahab excuse, yet allows the purified to lie 'with fear' when the moment calls). Against: Augustine (two whole treatises, the strongest case), Gregory the Great, Basil, Lactantius, John of Lycopolis, and Bishop Firmus as Augustine reports him. The rough pattern: Greek and Egyptian monastic writers mostly allowed deception in grave need, often calling it 'economy'; the Latin West after Augustine forbade every lie while calling the protective lie the lightest and most easily forgiven. The exceptions cut across that line: Basil is a strict Greek, and Hilary and Cassian are permissive Latins. Both camps hedge heavily. The permitters say last resort, with fear, a medicine not a food; the forbidders say the sin is small and the mercy behind it is rewarded. Both argue from the same stories: Rahab and the Hebrew midwives (Cassian: Rahab was saved for her lie; Augustine and Gregory: the midwives were rewarded for mercy, not for the lie, and only on earth).
splits_people_today: As worded, with a life at stake, the claim is one-sided today. The large majority of people, Christian or not, would agree: the killer at the door, or a family hiding Jews from the Nazis, is the standard example where nearly everyone approves the lie. The minority who disagree are principled rather than careless. Kant argued in 1797 that one may not lie even to the murderer. The Catholic Catechism teaches that lying is wrong by its nature (paragraphs 2482-2486), while saying no one is bound to reveal the truth to someone with no right to it (2489); so many careful Catholics answer 'refuse, stay silent, evade, but do not lie', which is Augustine's position. Some evangelical ethicists, Wayne Grudem among them, also hold that a spoken lie is never right. In The Hiding Place, Corrie ten Boom tells of her sister Nollie, who would not lie even to protect a hidden Jew. So the quiz gets a real split among Christians who think about it, but little split among the general public. People split more when the stakes are lower: lying to spare someone's feelings, to hide one's own good deeds, or to keep bad news from a sick person (Hilary, Clement and Chrysostom's physician all allow that last one, and modern medical ethics has turned against it).

misattributions.line: His teaching is that the master may lie, but the disciple must not.
misattributions.truth: Jerome's sarcastic summary of Origen (Apology against Rufinus 1.18, 401), not Origen's words. Origen's quoted fragment says whoever is under necessity may use falsehood with great care, like a medicine, and only for some great good.

misattributions.line: A Lie is Not Allowable, Even to Save Another from Injury.
misattributions.truth: A chapter heading supplied by editors and printed in the NPNF translation, not Augustine's sentence. His own words there: 'Nor are we to suppose that there is any lie that is not a sin, because it is sometimes possible, by telling a lie, to do service to another.'

misattributions.line: The truth is like a lion; you don't have to defend it. Let it loose; it will defend itself.
misattributions.truth: Not found in Augustine's works. It is a modern paraphrase, usually traced to Charles Spurgeon's remarks on defending the Bible (19th century).

misattributions.line: Ambrose held Judith's deed meritorious because 'she undertook for religion, not love... she served religion... and the fatherland'
misattributions.attributed_to: Ambrose of Milan (as cited in Wikipedia, 'Christian views on lying', as a summary of the tradition that defended lying)
misattributions.truth: Could not locate these words in the NPNF texts of On the Duties of the Clergy 3.13.82-88 or Concerning Widows 7.37-42. Ambrose does praise Judith's 'stratagem' and 'scheme', but he never discusses whether her lies to Holofernes were right. Treat as unverified, and do not count Ambrose on either side.

misattributions.line: Palladius of Antioch defended lying for a good cause
misattributions.attributed_to: Palladius (in Wikipedia's list of Fathers who defended lying)
misattributions.truth: No such figure is known in this debate; probably a garbled 'Palladius of Helenopolis'. Nothing on this was found in his Lausiac History or his Dialogue on the Life of Chrysostom.

notes:
1. The strongest pairing for a reveal is Hilary or Cassian against Augustine: each speaks directly to the same case, someone hiding and a killer asking. Cassian even asks the reader what he would do. Chrysostom is also strong, and in the pool, but his word is 'deceit' (apate) not 'lie', and his own case (tricking a friend into ordination) was for the friend's good rather than to save a life; Michal saving David is the protective example he gives.
2. Augustine's third way matters: 'I know where he is, but I will never show' (On Lying 24). An absolutist can refuse to answer, stay silent or accept torture; what he may not do is say something false. A quiz statement that forces a choice between lying and handing someone over (Cassian's framing) will sort people differently from one that allows silence (Augustine's framing).
3. Several permitters distinguish deceiving by action from lying in words (Ammonas sitting on the jar; Judith praised by Ambrose; Chrysostom's 'economy'). Some who reject verbal lies may accept protective deception by action.
4. Jerome is NOT placed. In his Commentary on Galatians (c. 386), following Origen, he read Paul's rebuke of Peter (Galatians 2) as a staged, 'useful pretence'. Augustine protested that this lets an 'officious lie' into Scripture (Augustine Letters 28, 40, 82). Jerome replied (Letter 112 = Augustine Letter 75) that he was 'not defending the use of falsehood in the interest of religion ... but teaching the honourable exercise of a wise discretion'. By c. 415 he read the rebuke as real (Augustine, Letter 180). In 401 he also mocked Origen for allowing lies (Apology against Rufinus 1.18). That debate is about the truth of Scripture, not lying to protect someone, and Jerome never gives a view on the hiding case.
5. Ambrose is NOT placed (see misattributions). Paulinus of Nola is listed by modern scholars (Ramsey 1985) in the 'permissive' tradition. The only relevant passage found is in his poem on St Felix (Carmen 16), where Felix, hunted by persecutors who fail to recognise him, says 'I do not know the Felix you are looking for'. That is self-protection, told as a miracle, and only in Walsh's copyrighted 1975 translation; not placed.
6. Dorotheus of Gaza (6th century, not in the pool) wrote a discourse 'On lying' that is reported to allow a lie only in grave necessity, rarely and with fear. The Greek text could not be found online (only an abridged modern Greek version that omits the passage), so it is not recorded. Status would be secondary-only.
7. A related but different question: refusing to lie to save one's OWN life by denying Christ. Justin Martyr: 'it is in our power, when we are examined, to deny that we are Christians; but we would not live by telling a lie' (First Apology 8, ANF vol. 1, newadvent.org/fathers/0126.htm). The martyrs are unanimous there, so it does not split the Fathers; do not use it for this claim.
8. Own renderings: Hilary and Climacus. Machine checks for these should compare the 'original' field against the url, after allowing for OCR noise in Hilary's archive.org text.
9. Heterodox: Origen (condemned after his death). All others in the stances are orthodox saints or respected writers. Clement is not in the current Roman Martyrology, but he was never condemned.
10. Suggested sharper contrast for the quiz writer: the Fathers disagree most visibly on whether a lie told to save a life is right, or only forgivable. Augustine and Gregory say forgivable but still a sin. Hilary, Chrysostom and Cassian say right, even required by love.
